doc.title: Joe LaBarbera interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 15, 2021

chapter: Time, feel and the move west
title: Moving to Los Angeles and not being a studio musician
summary: He moved west for family reasons, chose jazz over studio work, and knew the west coast scene from records.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Wow. What inspired your move to the west coast?

It really had to do with family considerations back then, You know I was married at the time to someone whose family was living in Phoenix, Arizona, they were getting older and she wanted to be closer to her parents. So I agreed to move west. I wanted to be in Los Angeles, you know, and our marriage started to fall apart for other reasons at the time, so in an attempt to not be too far away from my daughter, who was five at the time, I decided I’ll go to Los Angeles and see if I can make a go of it there. And that was probably the best decision I ever made.

Can you describe for me, I’m totally fascinated by the life of a studio musician and starting from the phone call, where that comes from be it X studio at this time and how much you know about the music and what is the expectation of the producer and all that stuff. That’s a long question.

It’s a long question and unfortunately you’re asking the wrong guy, Monk, ‘cause I’m not a studio musician. I never have been. I mean I made the mistake early on when we got to town — my wife and I’m, I’m remarried now and we’ve been together now for 26 years and we have a hard and fast rule of a vacation every year. And one year one of the big film composers in Los Angeles put out the call to me for a session, you know, and it goes through a service. So I’m talking to the person at the service, she’s saying so and so wants you for two days double scale, blah-blah-blah. And I said, “Oh gee, tell them thanks so much but you know I’m not available, we’re going on vacation.” And she was stunned. I mean she was literally like — she said, “Do you realize who this is?” I said, “Yeah,” but you know “we’ve got our tickets booked, we’re going” you know. So that pretty much ended any aspects — but I never really had a desire to do that. I came out here to play the music, which might seem insane at the time, but I realized that for decades there have been great jazz musicians on the west coast. My brothers and I grew up listening to all of the cats out here: Art Pepper, Bud Shank, Bill Perkins, you know Teddy Edwards, you name it. So I knew there was a scene here it just wasn’t maybe as viable as New York City, but it’s grown a lot over the years.
